For that the moon itself, which waxes and wanes, signifies the changeable nature of human flesh can be shown in many places of the Scriptures. These testimonies from the Psalms we have set down to show that the priesthood of the true Simon is most firm and everlasting.
52_marg3886: And king Antiochus sent, etc. This Antiochus, who was surnamed Sidetes, was the son of Demetrius Soter, and brother of the younger Demetrius, who reigned in Syria after Alexander Balas. Now Demetrius Soter reigned twelve years after Antiochus Eupator, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, as the chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome testifies. After him Alexander Philopator reigned ten years. After him Demetrius, the son of Demetrius, three years; who, taken by the Parthians, was thrust back into Hyrcania by king Arsaces. After him Antiochus Sidetes, brother of the same Demetrius, held the kingdom fourteen years. After his death it was restored again to Demetrius, who afterwards held it four years. But how the succession of the kingdom came about for the brothers Demetrius and Antiochus: it ought not to seem burdensome to the reader if I bring in something here from the History of Pompeius Trogus, who in the thirty-sixth book reports of this as follows. Antiochus, therefore, mindful that his father had been hated for pride, and his brother despised for sloth, lest he fall into the same vices, took Cleopatra, his brother’s wife, in marriage; he pursued with the greatest diligence the cities which had revolted at the beginning of his brother’s rule, and having subdued them added them again to the bounds of the kingdom; and he subdued the Jews, who under the Macedonian rule, in the time of Demetrius his father, had by arms claimed their liberty; and their strength was so great that after this they suffered no Macedonian king, and using their own rulers they harassed Syria with great wars. Likewise, in the thirty-eighth book, and the thirtieth, he joins these things to his former narrative. For Demetrius, as was said above, when he had made war on the Parthians, and had been victor in many engagements, was suddenly encircled by ambushes, lost his army, and was taken; Arsaces in Hyrcania not only gave him royal honor, but also gave him his daughter in marriage, and promised that the kingdom of Syria, which Tryphon had seized in his absence, should be restored. After the death of this man, his return despaired of, Demetrius, not bearing captivity, weary of a private life though wealthy, silently planned flight to his kingdom. His exhorter and companion was his friend Callimander, who after his captivity had come from Syria through the deserts of Arabia, guides having been bought with money, in Parthian dress, to Babylon. But as he fled, Phraates, who had succeeded Arsaces, by the swiftness of his horsemen along short cuts overtook and drew him back; and when he was brought to the king, Callimander was given not only pardon but also a reward for his fidelity; Demetrius, however, was severely chastised, and was sent back with his wife into Hyrcania, and ordered to be kept under closer guard. After an interval, when the children also that had been born gave a pledge of his loyalty, flight was attempted again with the same friend as companion. But with equal ill fortune he was caught near the end of his kingdom, and brought again to the king, that as one hated he might be removed from his sight. Then too, given back to his wife and children, he was sent back to Hyrcania, a city for him a punishment. And he was presented with golden dice in reproach of his boyish levity. But this so mild clemency of the Parthians toward Demetrius was caused not by the mercy of the nation, nor regard for kinship, but because they desired the kingdom of Syria, intending to use Demetrius against his brother Antiochus, as the matter, or the time, or the fortune of war should require. When he heard this, Antiochus, thinking he should seize the war first, led against the Parthians the army which he had hardened in many wars. But through luxury the equipage was no less than the soldiery; for eighty thousand armed men were followed by three hundred thousand camp-followers, of whom cooks and bakers were the greater number; and of silver and gold so much that even common soldiers fixed their boots with gold, and spurned the very material for love of which peoples fight with the sword. The kitchen utensils too were of silver, quite as if they were going to a banquet and not to war. When Antiochus came, many eastern kings met him, handing over themselves and their kingdoms with execration of Parthian pride. There was no delay in the engagement; Antiochus, victor in three battles, when he had seized Babylonia, began to be held great. And so, all peoples flocking to him, nothing was left to the Parthians but their ancestral borders. Then Phraates sent Demetrius into Syria with a Parthian guard to seize the kingdom, that by this arrangement Antiochus might be recalled to defend his own country; meanwhile, since he could not do so by force, he tried Antiochus everywhere with ambushes. Because of the multitude of men, Antiochus’s army was divided among the cities for winter quarters, and this was the cause of destruction. For when the cities saw themselves burdened by the exactions of supplies and the injuries of the soldiers, they revolted to the Parthians, and on the appointed day they attacked the army divided among them, by ambush, so that none could bring aid. When this was announced to Antiochus, he set out to bring help to the nearest, with the band which wintered with him. On the way he met the king of the Parthians, against whom he fought more bravely than his army did. But at last, though by valor he overcame the enemy, deserted through the fear of his own men, he was slain. For him Phraates held funeral rites in royal fashion, and the daughter of Demetrius, whom Antiochus had brought with him, he took as wife, captured by love of the maiden. Then he began to repent of having let Demetrius go, and to bring him back he had hurriedly sent squadrons of horse; but they found Demetrius, fearing this very thing, already in his kingdom, and having tried everything in vain they returned to their king. Antiochus’s army having been destroyed in Parthia, his brother Demetrius, freed from the Parthian siege and restored to the kingdom, when all Syria was in mourning because of the lost army, as if the wars in which one brother was captured and the other slain had been successfully waged by himself and his brother, resolved to make war on Egypt, Cleopatra his mother-in-law promising the kingdom of Egypt as the price of help against her brother. But, while he desired what was another’s, as usually happens, he lost his own through the revolt of Syria. For the Antiochenes first, under the leadership of Tryphon, execrating the pride of the king, which had become intolerable through the conversation of Parthian cruelty, then Apamea and the other cities, following the example, revolted from Demetrius in the king’s absence. Ptolemy also, king of Egypt, attacked by him in war, when he learned that his sister Cleopatra, with the wealth of Egypt put on ships, had fled to Syria to her daughter and to Demetrius her son-in-law, sent in a certain young Egyptian, son of the merchant Protarchus, to seek the kingdom of Syria even by arms, a story having been composed as if he had been received into the royal family by adoption of king Antiochus, and was not a Syrian, since they spurned any king whatever lest they suffer the pride of Demetrius. The name Alexander was put upon the young man, and great aid was sent from Egypt. Meanwhile the body of the slain Antiochus, sent back by the king of the Parthians in a silver coffin for burial in Syria, arrived. When it was received with great zeal by the cities and by king Alexander to confirm belief in the story, this won him great favor of the people, all thinking that tears not feigned were shed for them. But Demetrius, defeated by Alexander, when he was pressed by evils on every side, was at last deserted even by his wife and children. Left, therefore, with a few slaves, when he sought Tyre, intending to defend himself by the sanctity of its temple, he was killed as he disembarked from the ship by the governor’s command; for the causes aforesaid, etc. That Antiochus demands from Simon the cities possessed through battles signifies that the ancient enemy always envies the virtues of the saints and wishes to subject them to himself in unjust servitude; but Simon, the spiritual one, claiming them for himself, said they were his own right, and the inheritance of his fathers, and that the enemy ought to have no communion there, because the possession of virtues belongs properly to the elect, not to the reprobate. Whence the lands of the Chanaanites, into which the children of Israel are led, the sons of Sem had once obtained by lot in the division of the world; these afterwards the posterity of Cham possessed by force and power, through the iniquity of persuasion, in which too the most just judgment of God is proved. He both expelled those from the foreign places which they had wickedly occupied, and restored to these saints, as the possession of their fathers, that which had been assigned to their stock in the division of the world. This figure is known to stand in us also by the most certain reason. For the will of the Lord naturally assigned the possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After the prevarication of Adam, when the vices grew insolent, that is, the Chanaanite peoples were driven from their proper region, when by the grace of God they have again been restored to them by our diligence and labor, we are to believe that we have not so much occupied foreign lands as received back our own.
52_marg3887: And the king appointed. What is signified by Cendebeus, the captain of the sea coast, whom Antiochus sends to wage war on the Jews, if not the powers of this world and the persecutors of the Christian religion? Whom the mystical Antiochus, Antichrist, sends with an army of lictors and executioners to the destruction of the Christian people, that they may trample down the true Judea, that is, the Church, and take captive by error, or slay by blasphemy, the people of the faithful. Moreover Cendebeus is ordered to build Cedron. For Cedron is a torrent, or a valley near Jerusalem on the eastern side, which John the evangelist also mentions in the passion of the Lord. And Cedron was ordered to be built for this reason, that the gates of the city might be blocked and the people hemmed in. Cedron is interpreted sorrow, or grief, or pain. And fittingly he was ordered to build Cedron, to whom it was committed to inflict the pain of punishments on the confessors of Christ.
52_marg3888: And John went up, etc. We said above that Simon, the high priest, signified the prince of priests, namely him who by the obedience of the cross offered himself to the Father for us, whose two sons are the peoples of believers from the Jews and from the Gentiles. To these he commends the strength of war against all enemies and foes of the truth, that is, against Jews, pagans and heretics, and also against malignant spirits, that they may defend the Christian faith and protect the true confessors of God. Be you, he says, in my place, and my brethren, and go out and fight for our nation; and let the help from heaven be with you. Who are these brethren but those of whom the Truth itself, rising from the dead, says in the Gospel to the women visiting his sepulchre: “Go, tell my brethren that they go into Galilee, there they shall see me.” In the place, then, of Christ and the apostles are the saints, who, doing the will of the heavenly Father, seek the victory of the truth and the salvation of souls. Theirs is the help from heaven, from him assuredly of whom it is written in the Psalm: “God is wonderful in his saints: the God of Israel is he who will give power and strength to his people.” These chose twenty thousand fighting men, because they appoint only those as fit for spiritual warfare who become executors and doers of God’s commandments in the two precepts of charity.
52_marg3889: And he pitched his camp, etc. That this captain, when he saw the people afraid to go over the river, went over first, shows that those who act in the Church in the place of masters and in the office of teacher ought to strengthen by the example of their own faith and constancy the timidity of those subject to them, and to whet them for the battle line against the enemies with sacred trumpets, that is, with divine teachings; and so the spiritual Cendebeus and his camp are put to flight, and many of them fall wounded, because shaken with fear they at length feel the power of the divine majesty.
52_marg3890: Then was wounded, etc. That Judas was wounded in the battle and John pursued the enemies, signifies, unless I am mistaken, what Paul says: “Blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved,” because while the Jewish people delays in the faith of Christ, the Church of the Gentiles strongly presses the enemies, until she either converts the blind to repentance by saving compunction, or punishes those who persevere in wickedness by preaching to them with threats the future punishment. But when the times of the nations shall be fulfilled and their fullness shall have come in to the faith, then all Israel, that is, the whole Church from both peoples, will be saved by the gift of Christ through saving confession by faith, hope and charity.
52_marg3891: And Ptolemee. What is figured by Ptolemee, if not hypocritical and crafty men? These, then, attaching themselves to good masters with feigned discipline and pretending a piety whose power they utterly do not know, for the most part come to the honor of ecclesiastical dignity, the masters themselves bestowing it; for to be sons-in-law of the high priest is this: that those very persons whom the good masters regenerated with water and the word should receive a share in the power of their government. But when, having received the rank of their own power, they have begun each to be slaves to their desires, they strive by the circumventions of guile to supplant and overthrow the very honors of their benefactor, and they kill his sons and servants alike, since they spare no person living with them. But through money and flattery they gain the secular powers, and harass the Church with hidden snares or open persecutions. Nor is it a wonder that such wickedness can at times prevail in the Church, since we read that the head of the Church was handed over and taken captive to the Jews by the guile of the traitor Judas. Simon Magus was baptized by Philip, but was not purged from the wickedness of his mind. Julian the Apostate, raised up by the Church as a reader, persevered to the end of his life a savage enemy in the malice he had begun. Even the age of this time has not a few such, who, though they do not kill their masters with the sword, yet do not cease to persecute them with envy and hatred.
52_marg3892: And running before, etc. John indeed, his father having been slain by guile, guards himself more cautiously against the enemy and kills the men who had come to destroy him; so anyone, even of the number of the faithful saved by the grace of God, being provident and careful to preserve his own salvation, having heard of the deception practised by other enemies, strives to guard against their snares and to crush their perverse machinations. For simplicity alone does not suffice anyone for preserving his salvation, but with simplicity there ought equally to be prudence. Whence the Saviour says in the Gospel to the disciples: “Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves.” And the Apostle says: “Do not become children in sense: but in malice be children.” Simplicity, then, ought to be had by us, that we may harm no one; prudence also, that we be not despised by others; nor is there much difference between deceiving anyone and being able to be deceived by another.
52_marg3893: And the rest of the acts of John. This John, leader of the Jews and at once high priest, was a man of valour, and accomplished many wondrous works. He also, waging war against the Hyrcanians and conquering them, received the name of Hyrcanus; and asking of the Romans the right of friendship, by decree of the senate he was reckoned among their friends. But how Josephus tells of this same Hyrcanus, to make clear what is briefly said at the end of the book of Machabees, seems to us not unfitting to be set down here. For after he had at some point recalled the victory of Simon, he reports of his end thus: And he also dies at a banquet, taken by the treachery of Ptolemy his son-in-law, who, having shut up Simon’s wife and two sons in custody, sent trusted friends to kill John, the third, whose name was also Hyrcanus. But the young man, learning of the attack that was being prepared, hastened to the city, relying on the great multitude of the people, both for the memory of his father’s valour and because the wickedness of Ptolemy was hateful to all. Ptolemy wished to enter by another gate of the city, but was cast out by the people, who had received Hyrcanus sooner. And he indeed at once withdrew to a certain fortress beyond Jericho, which is called Dagon.
52_marg3894: Hyrcanus, however, obtained his father’s honour of the pontificate. After he had offered sacrifices to God, he quickly sought Ptolemy, intending to bring help to his mother and his brothers together; and having attacked the stronghold, he was superior in other matters, but yielded to a just grief. For whenever Ptolemy was pressed, he scourged his mother and brothers, led up onto the wall openly, so that they could be seen, and threatened to throw them down headlong unless he withdrew at once. Whence fear and pity moved Hyrcanus more than anger. But his mother, in no way terrified by the blows, but by the threatened death, stretching out her hands, begged her son that he should not, broken by the wrongs done to his own, let the wicked man escape; for she herself would count the death set before her by Ptolemy better than immortality, provided that he paid the penalty for the things he had done against right to her house. John, however, now considering his mother’s obstinacy and hearing her prayers, was impelled to rush upon him; then seeing her scourged and torn, he was made weak, and was wholly full of grief. Because of this, when the siege had been long drawn out, the sabbatical year came, which among the Jews it is the custom to keep as a rest in every seventh cycle, after the example of the seventh days. And in this Ptolemy, having got respite from the siege, killed the brothers of John together with their mother and fled to Zeno, who was surnamed Cotylas, tyrant of Philadelphia. But Antiochus, angry at what he had suffered through Simon, led an army into Judea, and sitting down there at Jerusalem, besieged Hyrcanus. But he, having opened the sepulchre of David, who had been the richest of kings, and taking from it more than three thousand talents of money, persuaded Antiochus, by the gift of three hundred talents, to depart from the siege; and he was the first of the Jews to begin to support foreign auxiliaries from private wealth. And again, when Antiochus, having undertaken war against the Medes, gave him time for vengeance, he at once advanced against the cities of Syria, thinking them empty of defenders, which was true. He took Medeba indeed and Samega with their neighbours, and also Shechem and Garizim, and besides these the race of the Cutheans, who dwell in the places adjoining the temple, built after the example of that which is at Jerusalem. He took also not a few other cities of Idumea, and besides Adora and Marisa. He advanced as far as Samaria, where the city Sebaste now is, founded by king Herod, and shut it in on every side, and set his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus over the siege. They, resisting not at all, came by the necessity of famine to the point that those who were within the city were forced to touch even unaccustomed flesh. So they called to their aid Antiochus, surnamed Spondius, who, when he had obeyed them with ready will, was overcome by Aristobulus and Antigonus, and he indeed fled as far as Scythopolis, the brothers, mentioned above, pursuing. But these, returning to Samaria, drove the multitude again within the wall, and having taken the city by storm they demolished it, and led away its inhabitants captive. But things being prosperously done in this way, they did not allow their eagerness to cool. But advancing quickly with the army as far as Scythopolis, they struck it also, and all the fields within Carmel were laid waste. In the second place, envy of the affairs of John and his sons stirred up a sedition of the nations, and many gathered against them and did not rest until they were conquered in open war. The remaining time of John, when he lived most fortunately, and administered affairs excellently for thirty years, he dies, three years having been administered, leaving five children, a man plainly most blessed, who had given no occasion for anyone to complain of his lot. In short, he alone had three things, and those the chief. For he was both prince of the nation, and high priest, and besides a prophet, with whom God conversed, so that he was altogether ignorant of nothing of things to come; for he also foresaw and foretold concerning his two elder sons that they would not remain in the Lord’s affairs. He held the pontificate itself after his father’s death, according to the faith of the chronicles, for twenty-six years. But his father Simon had been pontiff before him for eight years. Before him Jonathan, his brother, for eighteen years. Judas also, brother of Jonathan and Simon, held the pontificate for three years, although he had waged many wars before with the generals of the kings of Syria. After John, indeed, Aristobulus his son received the pontificate among the Jews, who, wishing also to become king at the same time, took the badge of the diadem, after four hundred and eighty-four years of the Babylonian captivity. He killed his brother Antigonus by treachery, and having completed one year in the kingdom, ended his life by the wretched death of a fratricide. His brother Anneus, who was also Alexander, succeeded him in the kingdom, which he held twenty-seven years so cruelly that, the people being provoked, he asked them what he could do to reconcile the people’s minds to himself. The answer was: if he were to die. For perhaps, having suffered such grave things at the hands of a dead man, they would return to favour, so as to lay aside their hatred against the departed. Roused by these things, and by the habit of rebelling, having killed many he drove the rest into a city whose name is Bethsel, and its capture brought a bitterer plague than usual, with so savage a course of cruelty that of that number he crucified eight hundred in the midst of the city. In their sight he ordered their wives and sons to be slaughtered. He looked on at this reclining in the midst of his concubines, merry among wine and cups, but drunk more with blood than with wine.
52_marg3895: By this deed alone he terrified the people more than by war, so that the next night eight thousand of the Jews went down beyond Judea, for whom the end of flight would be the death of Alexander. When he was dead, Alexandra his wife, who was also surnamed Salma, reigned in Jerusalem nine years. Thereafter, when the two brothers, sons of Alexander, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, were fighting over the rule, the Romans had occasion to invade Judea. So Pompey, at Hyrcanus' invitation, came to Jerusalem; the city taken and the temple opened, he went in as far as the holy of holies; he led with him Aristobulus, his younger brother, but confirmed the pontificate to Hyrcanus, and made Antipater, the father of Herod of Ascalon, procurator of Palestine. And so Hyrcanus, slothful in spirit, with the aid of the aforesaid procurator Antipater, held the pontificate thirty-four years. Afterwards, Antipater having been killed by poison at a banquet, Herod his son succeeded to the kingdom, who also killed Hyrcanus. Hence also Herod, son of the aforesaid Antipater of Ascalon and of his mother Cypris, an Arab, received the rule of the Jews from the Romans; in his time, the nativity of Christ being near, the kingdom and priesthood of Judea, which before had been held by succession of the lesser, was destroyed, the prophecy being fulfilled in which he speaks thus through Moses: “There shall not fail a prince out of Juda, nor a ruler from his thighs, till he come to whom it is laid up, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”
52_marg3896: In this place also Christ, whom the scripture of Daniel mentions beforehand, receives his end. For up to Herod the christs, that is, the priests, were kings of the Jews, who began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad and from the restoration of the temple under Darius, down to Hyrcanus and the hundred and eighty-sixth Olympiad, four hundred and eighty-three years having passed in between; which years Daniel also marks, saying: “And thou shalt know and understand, from the beginning of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem, unto the princedom of Christ, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” These sixty-nine weeks make four hundred and eighty-three years, in which the christs, that is, the priests consecrated by anointing, reigned down to Hyrcanus; he, last of all, having been taken by the Parthians, Herod the son of Antipater, who had no claim to Judea, received it from Augustus and the senate, and his sons reigned after him until the last captivity of Jerusalem, no pontiffs being appointed by succession of the priestly line, nor serving God for the duration of life according to the law of Moses. Certain ignoble men, and at another time others, and some for one year or a little more, bought the priesthood from the Romans. All which things the prophet Daniel also foretells, saying thus: “And after seven and sixty-two weeks” the chrism shall perish, “and judgment shall not be in him, and the people shall corrupt the holy temple with the leader that shall come, and they shall be cut down in the flood of war.” And in what follows: “And upon the temple,” he says, “shall be the abomination of desolations, and even to the consummation of the time, consummation shall be given upon the desolation.” Herod appointed a certain Ananelus, summoned from Babylon, high priest of the Jews, and after a short time gave Aristobulus, brother of his wife and grandson of Hyrcanus, as successor. When he had been killed after a year, he gave the priesthood back again to Ananelus. And now there was no lawful succession in the priesthood, but, the end of the law itself and of the priesthood drawing near, all things were in confusion. This Herod, moreover, was vigorous in the acts of war, in the government of the kingdom, and in the restoration of buildings, but of most unhappy and most cruel character. At Jerusalem he built many great houses. Samaria, long sitting in ashes, he raised up from the foundations in honor of Augustus; he called it Augusta, that is, Sebaste, and in Pamis he built the temple which is called Pamon. He founded Caesarea in the name of Caesar, which was formerly called the Tower of Strato. He founded besides Antidana and Antipatris, and built Herodium, in honor of his father Antipater and of himself. Countless works also he built with great skill in the several cities which he ruled. But amid these things he killed Hyrcanus, who had once been priest of the Jews, on his return from the Parthian captivity, and his son, who had succeeded his father in the priesthood. He also most cruelly killed the sister of the latter, his own wife, with two sons of his own, already youths, and the mother of the wife he had slain, his mother-in-law. Indeed Herod himself, lest he be thought ignoble and perhaps be charged as a stranger to the seed of the Jews, burned all the books in which the nobility of the Jewish nation was kept written in the temple, so that, the proofs failing, he too might be thought to belong to it. Moreover, to mingle his offspring with their royal race, having cast off Doris, a woman of Jerusalem, whom he had taken as wife while a private man, and Antipater, the son born of her, he joined to himself Mariamne, daughter of Alexander, granddaughter of Aristobulus the brother of Hyrcanus, who before him was king of the Jews. She bore him five sons, of whom two, Alexander and Aristobulus, he himself killed in Samaria, and without delay afterwards he destroyed with a like crime their mother also, than whom he had known nothing dearer. Of these, Aristobulus had begotten as his son Herod, by Berenice, whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles was struck by an angel. He also added to what he had cruelly done above this: that he killed the husband of his sister Salome. And when he had given her to another, he killed this man also, as her husband. He also slew the scribes, interpreters of the divine law, with a like crime.
52_marg3897: But when he had learned, from the information of the magi, of the birth of Christ our Lord, who was born in Bethlehem in the thirty-second year of his reign, he ordered all the little ones to be killed. But after he had completed the thirty-seventh year of his reign, he died a death marvelously fitting, of a dropsy under the skin, with worms bursting forth over his whole body. How Josephus tells of the end of Herod does not seem unfitting to bring into this little work of ours; he relates it in this way. For he had a fever, not a moderate one, and an intolerable itching held the whole surface of his body. He was vexed with continual torments of the colon, and his feet had swollen as from the fault of water under the skin; moreover the swelling of the belly, and the rotting of the testicles breeding little worms, and besides frequent panting, and broken sighs, and a contraction of all his limbs wearied him, so that those who referred these things to the divinity said that they were the punishments of the sophists. But he, although he struggled with the torments of so many ills, was nevertheless desirous of life, and hoped for health by remedies he had devised. At last, having crossed the Jordan, at Callirrhoe he used hot waters, which flowing into a lake rich in bitumen, called Asphaltites, were drunk for their sweetness. There his body, which the physicians had decided to foment with warmer oil, was plunged into a vessel full of it, and was so dissolved that he rolled his eyes loose like a dead man. Then those who were attending him were thrown into confusion, and he seemed to look toward their outcry. But despairing of health, he ordered fifty drachmas to be divided to each of the soldiers, and much money among the officers and friends. And when, returning, they had come to Jericho, seized with black bile, and himself nearly changed to death, he devised a necessary deed; for he commanded that the nobler men of every city of all Judea be gathered and shut up in a place called the Hippodrome. Then, having called to him his sister Salome and Alexander her husband, he said: I know that the Jews will celebrate that death of mine with festal joys; but I can be mourned by others, and gain most illustrious honors of burial, if you do what I command. These men, who are held in custody, when I have breathed out my soul, surround with soldiers and kill at once, so that all Judea, hateful to me, and every house may weep for me. And at the same time, with these commands given, letters were brought from the envoys whom he had sent to Rome, in which it was reported that Acme the handmaid had been put to death by command of Caesar, and that Antipater was condemned to death. Yet it was also written that if the father preferred to send him into exile, Caesar had permitted it. But Herod, a little revived by this news and again overcome by pains, for he was racked by hunger and cough alike with violence, tried to reach his breath. And having taken an apple, he also asked for a knife, for he was accustomed to eat it cut. Then, looking around lest anyone should hinder him, he raised his right hand as if to strike himself. But when Achiabus his cousin had run up and held back his hand, a very great wailing was raised in the palace at once, as if the king were dead. And Antipater, having quickly heard this, regained confidence, and now glad, with money also sent ahead, begged the guards to release and dismiss him. Their chief not only prevented this from being done, but even quickly told the king. He, crying out more strongly than the strength of a sick man could manage, at once sent guards and killed Antipater, and commanded that he be buried, dead, in Hyrcania. Then he again corrected his will, and wrote as successor Archelaus, the eldest brother of Antipater, and Antipas as tetrarch. And after the death of his son, five days having passed, he died, in the thirty-fourth year from when he killed Antigonus and gained the kingdom, and the thirty-seventh after he was declared king by the Romans. He died therefore in the forty-seventh year of the empire of Augustus; in his place his son Archelaus, appointed by Augustus, reigned nine years until the end of Augustus himself.
52_marg3898: For then, the Jews no longer enduring his ferocity but accusing him before Augustus, he was banished to Vienne, a city of Gaul; and to lessen the power of the Jewish kingdom and tame its insolence, four brothers were appointed tetrarchs in his place: Herod, Antipater, Lysias and Philip. Of these, Philip and Herod, who was formerly called Antipas, had been ordained tetrarchs even while Archelaus was alive. But after Archelaus, Herod, tetrarch of the Jewish nation, held the principality twenty-four years, when the emperor Tiberius had given him this power; in the twelfth year of Tiberius, Pilate was sent by the same emperor as procurator of Judea, and he continued there ten years together, almost to the very end of Tiberius. But in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and likewise the fifteenth of the reign of Herod, as the histories tell, John, the son of Zachary, preaching in the desert near the river Jordan, bears witness that Christ the Son of God is present in the midst of them; and the aforesaid Herod, at the urging of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, ordered him beheaded at a banquet at the request of a dancing girl, as the holy Gospel plainly shows. The Lord Jesus Christ himself also announces the way of salvation here among the people, proving by signs and miracles that what he said was true. Likewise, in the eighteenth year of both principalities, Jesus Christ, according to the prophecies that had been spoken beforehand of him, came to the Passion. There, presented to this Herod by Pilate’s envoys, not received with faith but scorned through worldly pride, clothed in a white garment, he was sent back again to Pilate, by whom, through the service of the soldiers, he was crucified, and on the third day rose again from the dead. Now divine Scripture relates that the beginning of the preaching of the gospel was made in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and he maintained that Jesus himself spent the whole time of his teaching under the high priests Annas and Caiphas. In these spaces scarcely four whole years are contained. The legal precepts were by then ceasing, and through ambition; for the honor of the priesthood was given to no one for merit of life or of birth. But by Roman power the highest priesthood was now granted to some, now to others, so that they were changed in yearly successions. Finally, the same Josephus relates that four in order, after Annas, discharged the office of the pontificate up to Caiphas, writing in these words: Valerius Gracchus, having removed Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ismael, the son of Bassus, high priest. But rejecting him also not long after, he put Eleazar, the son of the high priest Ananias, in the pontificate in his place. After a year he also removes him from the office and handed over the ministry of the pontificate to one Simon, the son of Canisus. He too having discharged it no longer than the space of one year, received as successor Joseph, otherwise Josippus, who was also named Caiphas. And by this the whole time in which our Lord and Saviour is described as having taught on earth is confined within the space of four years, in which these four successions of high priests, which Josephus records, are described as scarcely serving one year each. But how Herod the tetrarch lost his kingdom Josephus tells, saying: The accuser of Herod the tetrarch, Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, whom Herod’s father killed, came to Tiberius. But he not receiving the accusation, and staying at Rome, he sought the notice of some powerful men. But he cultivated with the greatest services Gaius, the son of Germanicus, while he was still a private man; and one day, amid a plentiful provision of feasts at which he was being entertained by him, at the end, with hands stretched out, he openly began to pray to God that he might quickly see him lord of all, Tiberius being dead. When one of his intimates had reported this to Tiberius, he at once ordered Agrippa to be shut up. He was kept in prison under great hardship for six months, until the death of Tiberius. But when he was dead, after a reign of twenty-two years and three days, Gaius Caesar, succeeding to the empire, released Agrippa from his chains and gave him the tetrarchy of Philip, for the latter had by then died, and called him king. And when he had come to his kingdom, Agrippa stirred up through envy the desires of Herod the tetrarch. Herodias his wife chiefly provoked him to hope for the kingdom, reproaching him with his concord and saying: That through not having been willing to sail to Caesar he lacked greater power; for since he had made Agrippa a king from a private man, how could he hesitate to give him, a tetrarch, the same honor? Led on by these things, Herod came to Gaius, by whom, for his avarice, he was sharply rebuked, and fled to Spain. For the accuser Agrippa had followed, and Gaius also added Herod’s tetrarchy to him. And so Herod, living abroad in Spain, died with his wife Herodias also with him. But Pontius Pilate, the governor, in the same year in which the Saviour suffered, secretly by night set up the images of Caesar in the temple, as Josephus tells. And this was the cause of the first sedition and troubles for the Jews.
52_marg3899: But afterwards, spending the sacred treasure, which the Jews call Corban, on an aqueduct of Jerusalem, he gave the seeds of a second sedition. But when the same Pilate reported to Tiberius concerning the teaching of the Christians, and recalled some things of the deeds of the Redeemer himself, his passion and resurrection, Tiberius referred it to the senate, that he might be received among the other sacred things. But when, by the decree of the fathers, Tiberius had decided that the Christians be removed from the city, he threatened death by edict to the accusers of the Christians. Tertullian writes in the Apologeticus that many of the Roman senators and knights were put to death by the same. Therefore divine vengeance condemned the Jews for the crime committed. But Pilate himself also, who performed the office of an unjust judge against the Saviour, in the same times of Gaius was tormented with such and so great disasters of evils that he is reported to have pierced himself through with his own hand and by violence cast away his wicked life. For he could not escape unpunished for so great a crime, as we find in the histories of the Greeks, of those at least who write the Olympiads and compose annual books of things done for the memory of posterity. But Agrippa, who also was Herod, son of Aristobulus, after the killing of James the son of Zebedee, sent the apostle Peter into prison and stirred up persecution against those believing in Christ, but did not escape unpunished, as Luke makes plain in the Acts of the Apostles, and Josephus recalls in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities, who relates of him in this manner: He had completed, he says, the third year of his rule over all Judea, when by chance he came to Caesarea, which was formerly called Strato’s Tower. There he put on spectacles for the citizens in honour of Caesar, on a day of vows, as it seemed, for Caesar’s safety. And when the men of the whole province, endowed with honour and means, had assembled there, on the second day of the spectacles, clothed in a shining robe wonderfully woven of gold and silver, at the beginning of the day he proceeds to the theatre, where, when the silver garment had first received the rays of the sun in its bosom, the brilliance of the quivering metal poured forth a light doubled for the spectators by the reflected splendour, so that the terror of the sight dazzled the eyes of those looking, and through this their arrogance, the artificer, feigned something more of him than is of human nature. At once the voices of the flattering crowd ring out, sounding honour but bringing destruction, and from this side and that the crowds cry out from the benches that he be called God, and he is humbly entreated to be gracious, the peoples saying: Until now we have held you as a man, but from this time we confess that you are above human nature. But the king did not check the acclamation held against what is right, nor shrank from the impiety of the unlawful flattery, until, looking up a little after, he saw an angel hanging over and standing above his head, and he perceived him at once to be the minister of his destruction, whom before he had not known as the provider of honours. And behold, suddenly a torment seized him, from an incredible pain of the belly, and a swelling. And looking to his friends he said: Behold, I, your God, am at once driven forth and thrown down from life, since a certain divine power has convicted the false voices lately bestowed on me, and I, who was just now called immortal by you, am now hurried headlong into death. But the sentence which God has appointed must be accepted, and we have lived either to be despised, or have fulfilled the length of life which was thought blessed. And when he had said this, being more violently tossed by the force of the pain, he was at once carried back to the palace. And when it was spread abroad that he would die within a few days, a huge multitude of every age and sex, assembling according to the custom of the fathers, besought almighty God for the king’s safety, lying prostrate at the edge of his couch. And the whole royal house resounded with lamentations and groans. Meanwhile the king himself, lying in an upper chamber, and looking down, and seeing all prostrate and bowed down with weeping, did not himself refrain from tears; but, tormented for five continuous days by pains of the belly, he violently broke off his life, in the fifty-fourth year of his age and the seventh of his reign; for he had reigned four years under Gaius Caesar, holding the tetrarchy of Philip for three years, and in the fourth adding also that of Herod, and the other three years having passed under Claudius Caesar. After Agrippa the father, who held the kingdom of Judea for seven years, his son Agrippa was put in the kingdom by Claudius, which he held for twenty-six years, that is, up to the second year of Vespasian, when the destruction of the city took place. But how Josephus tells of this, we think should be set down in this place: Claudius, he says, appointed Agrippa, son of Agrippa, king of the Jews, but sent Felix as procurator of the whole province, of Samaria also and Galilee and the region called Transjordan. And after a few words he added this also: A most bitter sedition is also kindled by the high priests against the priests and the chief men of the people of Jerusalem, each of whom, complaining to themselves, set themselves up as leaders of their own faction, with bands of ruined young men rejoicing in revolutions. These, clashing with one another, first provoked each other with abuses, then afterwards struck each other down with stones, and there was no one to restrain them, but all things were done as in a city having no ruler. So the high priests came to such want that they sent their servants to the threshing-floors and seized the tithes which were owed to the priests; and it happened that some of the lesser priests, whose food had been taken by force, perished of hunger. So the violence of the seditions had confounded right and wrong. Likewise after a few words he adds this also: Sometimes also in the midst of the city they slew those who met them, especially on feast days, the assassins mingling with the crowds and going about with daggers hidden, so that whoever was marked out by them, if he came close, they killed him; and by wicked art, when he had fallen whom they had struck down with a secret wound, the murderers themselves proudly pretended to be indignant against those who committed such things in the midst of the city, and in this way their hidden crimes remained concealed; and first of all by them Jonathan the high priest was killed. After him very many were butchered, so that the fear of death was now heavier than the deaths themselves, while each one, as if always set in readiness, hoped at every moment to be killed.
52_marg3900: When Claudius, having completed fourteen years in the empire, with seven months and twenty-eight days, had died, Nero received the empire, which he held fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In his second year Festus, procurator of Judea, succeeded Felix; by him Paul is sent bound to Rome, and remaining two years in free custody, after this is released to preach, Nero not yet breaking out into such crimes as the histories relate of him. James, the brother of the Lord, when he had ruled the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years, was stoned in the seventh year of Nero by the Jews, who were avenging on him that they had been unable to kill Paul. Albinus succeeded Festus as governor of Judea; Florus succeeded Albinus, whose luxury and avarice and other shameful deeds the Jews could not bear, and they rebelled against the Romans. Against them Vespasian, the master of the soldiery, was sent and took very many cities of Judea. Nero first, above all his crimes, also persecuted the Christians. Of them he killed the most eminent at Rome, Peter by the cross, Paul by the sword. He, venturing nothing at all by the right of war, almost lost Britain; for two most noble towns were taken and overthrown there under him. Finally Nero, when he was being sought by the senate for punishment, fleeing from the palace, killed himself at the fourth milestone from the city, in the suburban house of his freedman, between the Salarian and Numentan roads, in the thirty-second year of his age; and in him the whole family of Augustus was ended.
52_marg3901: After Nero, Galba in Spain, Vitellius in Germany, and Otho at Rome seized the empire. Galba, in the seventh month of his reign, was beheaded in the middle of the forum of the city of Rome. Vespasian drove the Jews, overcome in two battles, back to their walls. Otho, in the third month of his reign, at Vitriacum, otherwise Venatrum, fell by his own hand. Vitellius, the seventh of the Romans, is cast into the Tiber by the generals of Vespasian. Vespasian reigned eight years, eleven months, twenty-two days; he was called emperor by the army among the Jews, and committing the war to his son Titus, he set out for Rome by way of Alexandria. In his second year Titus, Judea being taken and Jerusalem overthrown, killed six hundred thousand men. Josephus, however, who knew it, affirms that six hundred thousand men perished by the sword and famine, and another hundred thousand captives were publicly sold. He relates that the cause of so great a multitude being found at Jerusalem was the feast of unleavened bread. For this reason the Jews, flocking to the temple from every nation, were shut up in the city as in a prison. For it was fitting that they should be put to death in the same days of the Pasch in which they had crucified the Saviour. Now the whole time is reckoned to the second year of Vespasian; and the last overthrow of Jerusalem is forty-two years from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and from the beginning of the preaching of the gospel; two hundred and thirty-eight years from the captivity which they suffered under Antiochus; five hundred and ninety years from the second year of Darius, under whom the temple was built again; and from the first building of the temple under Solomon to its last ruin, which was made under Vespasian, one thousand one hundred and two years. Here ends the first book of Machabees.
